content.passage: YEMENIA began flying on 1st January, 1961. In those days, it was a domestic airline. Its base was in Taiz and it flew to places like Aden, Hodeidah, Barat and Sana'a. content.passage:
Ahmed Said was born in Taiz. He is one of seven children. At secondary school his best subjects were English and history. As a student he listened to the radio, watched TV and read every newspaper he could get his hands on. Then he went to Sana'a University. He took a degree in journalism. He has worked as a journalist for two years. Now, at the age of twenty-five, he is going to England to continue his studies at Exeter University.

Exeter is a city in the south-west of England. When I asked Ahmed why he had chosen Exeter, he said, "Exeter is about the same size as Sana'a. It has a local newspaper, TV station and radio station. It brings news to ordinary people in the area. They tell people what is happening in their area. That's what I am interested in and that's what I want to do. London is too big. That's why I didn't want to go there."

---

Paul Archer was born in Manchester. He is one of three children. At secondary school his best subjects were mathematics and history. As a student he was interested in buildings, old and new. Then he went to Cardiff University. He took a degree in architecture. He has worked as an architect for twenty-five years. Now, at the age of fifty, he is going to Sana'a. He will work with Yemeni architects restoring old buildings.

When I asked him why he had chosen Sana'a, he said, "The old buildings in Sana'a are wonderful. There is nothing like them anywhere in the world. I will learn a lot and maybe I can help a little bit. That's why I want to go there."

Fifteen minutes later we were driving along the bumpy road to the fort at Sharjah. It was a magnificent building with huge iron doors and a large courtyard. I hurried to my room, had a quick wash and then watched the desert sunset. It was a sight that I will never forget.

activities.title: Grammar: Past Simple vs. Present Perfect
activities.instruction: Read the rule about past tenses. Then, Challenge yourself! 📝 Select the best option for the correct verb form to complete each sentence.
activities.compensates: Teacher-led grammar explanation and oral drills (Teacher Guide, section 1A and 1B).

options.feedback: Great! Remember: Present Perfect is for an unknown time in the past. Past Simple is for a specific, known time.

questions.question: Study this rule from your workbook before you start.
questions.explanation: We use the Present Perfect (have/has + past participle) to talk about actions in the past when the time is not specific. We use the Past Simple to talk about actions that happened at a specific time in the past (e.g., yesterday, last week, in 2010).

options.feedback: Correct! We don't know the specific time, so we use the Present Perfect.
Not quite. We use the Past Simple when we know the exact time, like 'yesterday' or 'last year'.

questions.question: Hussein _______ to many interesting places.

Excellent! 'Last year' is a definite time, so we use the Past Simple.

questions.question: He _______ a racing car last year.
questions.explanation: The phrase 'last year' indicates a specific time, so the Past Simple 'drove' is correct.

options.feedback: Try again. The word 'ever' is a clue that we are asking about any time in the past, not a specific time.
Perfect! We use 'Have you ever...?' to ask about experiences at any time in life.

questions.question: ______ you ever ______ in a submarine?
questions.explanation: To ask about experiences at an indefinite time in the past, we use the Present Perfect structure 'Have you ever...?'

activities.title: Making Polite Requests
activities.instruction: Read the response and Challenge yourself! 📝 Select the best option for the most appropriate polite request that someone probably asked.
activities.compensates: The Teacher Guide activity where students think of requests for given responses.

options.text: Do you mind if I open the window?
options.feedback: Correct. 'Not at all' is a common polite response to a 'Do you mind...?' question.
Incorrect. A more likely response to 'Can you...?' would be 'Yes, of course' or 'Sure'.
This is a question asking for a reason, not a request.

questions.question: Response: 'Not at all. Please, go ahead.'
questions.explanation: The phrase 'Do you mind if I...?' is a polite way to ask for permission. 'Not at all' means 'I don't mind'.

options.text: Do you like cleaning your car?
options.feedback: This is a question about preference, not a request for help.

options.text: Would it be possible for you to help me with my homework?
options.feedback: Correct. This is a polite request for help, and the response gives a reason for being unable to help.
The response answers this question, but it's not a request.

questions.question: Response: 'I'm sorry, I can't. I'm cleaning my car.'
questions.explanation: 'Would it be possible for you to...?' is a very polite way to ask someone to do something. The response 'I'm sorry, I can't' is a polite refusal with a reason.

options.text: Could you help me lift this heavy box?
options.feedback: Correct. This request involves physical effort, and hurting one's back is a good reason to refuse.

options.text: Would you mind telling me the time?
options.feedback: Incorrect. Telling the time doesn't require physical effort, so this response wouldn't make sense.

options.text: How did you hurt your back?
options.feedback: This is a question asking for information, not a request for action.

questions.question: Response: 'I'm sorry. I've hurt my back.'
questions.explanation: A polite request like 'Could you help me...?' can be refused politely by giving a valid reason, like an injury.
